catalog_quote: Hup also has two contrastive tones, realized on stressed syllables, and prosodic nasalization, by which most morphemes are entirely nasal or entirely oral. [p. 450] ... a) The canonical (and minimal, as noted below) monomorphemic prosodic word is a single CVC syllable with one stress/tone locus; e.g. mɔ̌y ‘house’. b) Monomorphemic words with two syllables are much less frequent and normally take the form CV1CV1C ... Again, there is only one stress/tone locus, which occurs almost without exception on the second syllable. [p. 470] ... e) ... they have maximally one to two primary stress/tone loci, which normally occur on the boundary suffix and/or on the syllable that precedes it (with one or two exceptional patterns, which are also lexically determined by the boundary suffix). [p. 471] ... In verbs, as noted above, multimorphemic strings maximally take between one and two primary stress/tone loci. These normally occur on the boundary suffix and/or on the preceding syllable, as seen in example (33) and many others above. [p. 473] ... For nouns, the principal stress/tone domain spans positions 5-15, but the identity of elements as roots, adjectives, classifiers, or particular suffixes determines which syllables will attract stress. As with verbs, stress in the nominal construction is normally culminative, but certain suffixes are lexically marked to receive an additional stress. [p. 474]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hup is a word-accent (tonal-accent) language: a high (with falling allophone) or rising tone is realised on the stressed syllable. Roots are canonically one CVC syllable carrying the single stress/tone locus; the rare bisyllabic and reduplicated roots stress the second (final) syllable. In inflected verbs there are one or two primary stress/tone loci, normally on the obligatory boundary suffix and/or the syllable before it, the choice being lexically fixed by that suffix; in noun phrases stress is culminative over the whole phrase (demonstrative+noun, noun+adjective take one primary stress) and its locus depends on the identity of roots, adjectives, classifiers and suffixes. So stress is right-edge oriented but morphologically determined rather than counted from the word edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the source speaks only of 'one or two primary stress/tone loci' per domain (verb complex or noun phrase) and of certain nominal suffixes 'lexically marked to receive an additional stress' (p. 474).
new_statements.exceptions: The 'filler' suffix -Vw and the inchoative -ay never receive stress/tone (p. 473); enclitics are unstressed CVC morphemes whereas particles (after position 26) receive independent stress/tone (pp. 460, 473); pre-verbal pronominal subjects are unstressed and in the Upper Rio Tiquié dialect reduced to tV- (p. 455); an incorporated simplex O between a valence-adjusting preformative and the verb is unstressed while the preformative then receives stress/tone (pp. 458, 473); 'one or two exceptional patterns' of locus placement, lexically determined by the boundary suffix (p. 471).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic/grammatical word rather than the phrase for verbs (stress/tone domain = verb-complex positions 2/3-26, i.e. root(s) through boundary suffix and enclitics) but the noun phrase for nouns (positions 5-15; one primary stress per NP). Examples are from Epps's naturalistic corpus and elicitation (Tiquié-river Hup, Brazil); the same conventions are stated to follow Epps 2008a, which is the fuller treatment. Ramirez 2006 (p. 33) independently confirms the two-tone (high vs rising) contrast but says nothing about stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: The description is of Hup proper (hupd1244), Epps's corpus from the Tiquié-river communities in Brazil (dialects Tat Dëh, Barreira, Umari Norte, Nova Fundação); one dialect-specific note concerns Upper Rio Tiquié pronoun reduction. Giacone 1955 calls the language 'Ubde-Nehern ou Macú' and Moore & Franklin 'Makú-Hupda'; all the same language. Sister language Yuhup (yuhu1238) is treated separately in the literature (Lopes & Parker 1999) and was not used here.

new_statements.quote: [ms p. 3] Where lexemes have more than one syllable, primary stress falls on the final syllable. […] [ms p. 4] In all four languages, only one long vowel and/or contrastive tone is realized per morpheme (and, in most cases, also per phonological word), and always coincides with stress. […] Such tonal systems that are parasitic on lexical stress have been characterized as 'word-accent' systems […] [§3.2, ms p. 7] As in Dâw, stress in Hup and Yuhup is consistently stem-final (word-final when no bound morphology is present). There are two contrastive tonal categories in each language, and (as in Dâw) tone is only contrastive on stressed syllables. Vowel length plays no phonological role in the system. In Hup, the two contrastive tones are high and rising (6-7; see Epps 2008: 89).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (+, 24-pp. HAL deposit of Diachronica ms DIA-24045R2, title page 'Tonogenesis in the Naduhup family of northwest Amazonia', Simmons & Epps) is held by the project. All quoted sentences found verbatim in the text layer: ms p. 3 (the text layer) 'Where lexemes have more than one syllable, primary stress falls on the final syllable.'; ms p. 4 (the text layer) 'In all four languages, only one long vowel and/or contrastive tone is realized per morpheme (and, in most cases, also per phonological word), and always coincides with stress.'.. 'Such tonal systems that are parasitic on lexical stress have been characterized as word-accent systems (Riad 1998; Remijsen & van Heuven 2005)'; section 3…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Epps 2024 statement (two contrastive tones realized on stressed syllables, one stress/tone locus per prosodic word); adds the explicit placement (stem-final, word-final absent bound morphology; family-wide 'primary stress falls on the final syllable'), the word-accent characterization, and the irrelevance of vowel length. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so this supplies the placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hup word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the stem (word-final when no bound morphology follows); the language has two lexical tones (high vs rising, high with a falling allotone) that contrast only on that stressed syllable, so there is exactly one obligatory H pitch per phonological word and unstressed syllables take default low pitch: a 'word-accent' system in which tone is parasitic on stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described for Hup; the paper speaks only of one primary stress / one H per phonological word (secondary stress is mentioned only for Scandinavian as a typological parallel).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone has a reduced contrastive load on verbs (limited to certain grammatical functions such as imperative and deverbal derivation, and certain suffixes); fn. 7: Hup 'exhibits high pitch as a correlate of stress' in morphologically complex (mainly verbal) constructions, outside the tonal system; in stressed open syllables only high tone occurs and the vowel is allophonically lengthened.
new_statements.identity_note: Simmons & Epps 2025 treat Hup as a whole (data from Epps's 2001- corpus, Brazilian Hup of the Tiquie/Vaupes region) alongside Yuhup, Daw and Nadeb; the family-wide sentence 'primary stress falls on the final syllable' covers all four Naduhup languages, and §3.2 is specific to Hup and Yuhup. Moore 1977 describes Hupda as spoken at Pocawa on the Papuri river, Colombia (three speakers, 1970-1974).
